Using mai from R

Source: vignettes/rmai.Rmd
rmai.Rmd

mai is the compiled statistical computing language from Brendan McArdle’s 2018 University of Auckland PhD thesis. It reads like R, but compiles loops and function calls to fast bytecode. rmai lets you use it from R.

Getting the executable 

rmai::mai_install()          # downloads mai-lib/mai and builds it (Linux)
rmai::mai_install("~/src/mai", portable = TRUE)   # or from a local checkout

mai_path() shows which executable rmai will use. You can also point it at one with options(rmai.path = "/path/to/mai") or the MAI_PATH environment variable.

mai_available()
#> [1] TRUE

Running code 

mai_run("print(sum(1:100))")
#> 5050

mai_run(c(
  "const harmonic = function(int n) : double {",
  "    var s = 0.0",
  "    for(int i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) s = s + 1.0 / i",
  "    s",
  "}",
  "print(harmonic(1000000))"
))
#> 14.392727

Errors in mai code become R warnings by default (error = "stop" makes them R errors):

out <- mai_run('stop("something went wrong")')
#> Warning: mai: stop: something went wrong
attr(out, "error")
#> [1] "stop: something went wrong"

mai_source("script.mai") runs a file, with include paths resolved relative to the file’s directory.

Passing R data in and getting R values back

mai_eval() is the most natural way to use mai from R. Named arguments become const globals in mai, the expression is evaluated there, and the result comes back as an R vector or array. Data moves in binary, so doubles are exact and large inputs are cheap.

x <- runif(1e5)
mai_eval("sum(sqrt(x))", x = x)
#> [1] 66643.22
sum(sqrt(x))
#> [1] 66643.22

The expression can be a whole block. Here a loop that would be slow in plain R runs as compiled mai, with a helper defined in .setup:

mai_eval(
  "var n = length(x), s = 0.0
   for(int i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) s = s + sq(x[i] - 0.5)
   s / n",
  x = x,
  .setup = "const sq = function(double v) : double v * v"
)
#> [1] 0.08314382

Integer and logical vectors keep their types, matrices keep their shape, and NA survives the trip:

m <- matrix(c(1, NA, 3, 4), 2)
mai_eval("m * 10.0", m = m)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   10   30
#> [2,]   NA   40
mai_eval("!b", b = c(TRUE, NA, FALSE))
#> [1] FALSE    NA  TRUE

mai chunks in R Markdown and Quarto

Loading rmai registers a mai knitr engine. Each chunk runs in a fresh mai process. To build on an earlier chunk, label it and name it in mai.include:

```{mai, helpers}
const dotprod = function(x, y) sum(x * y)
const norm = function(x) sqrt(dotprod(x, x))
```
const dotprod = function(x, y) sum(x * y)
const norm = function(x) sqrt(dotprod(x, x))
```{mai, mai.include = "helpers"}
print(norm(vec(3.0, 4.0)))
```
print(norm(vec(3.0, 4.0)))
#> 5.0

Comparing with R

mai_compare() times a run() function defined in each language:

mai_compare(
  "const fib = function(n) if(n <= 2) 1 else fib(n - 2) + fib(n - 1)
   const run = function() fib(24)",
  "fib <- function(n) if (n <= 2) 1 else fib(n - 2) + fib(n - 1)
   run <- function() fib(24)",
  reps = 3
)
#>   language  seconds  speedup
#> 1      mai 0.011903 3.192472
#> 2        R 0.038000 1.000000

See the mai documentation, especially “Differences from R”, before writing much mai: for example 7 / 2 is 3, and assigning to an undeclared variable inside a function sets a global.
